title: Worry, by Appointment: A Small Practice for Thoughts That Keep Returning
subtitle: A short, scheduled window can give recurring concerns a place to be considered—without pretending that every worry can be solved or switched off.

body: A concern can show up while you are answering a message, walking to the bus or trying to enjoy dinner. Sometimes there is a practical issue to address; sometimes the mind is rehearsing a possible future without producing new information. Either way, repeatedly taking up the thought can make it feel as if it must be handled right now. A scheduled worry window offers another option: note the concern, choose a time to revisit it, and return to what you were doing if that feels possible. The aim is not to prove the worry wrong or force it away. It is to create a boundary around when you engage with it. Think of the appointment as a small experiment in attention, not a promise of calm, and certainly not a test of whether you are worrying correctly.

The distinction matters. If a worry arrives before your chosen time, write down a few words that will help you recognize it later: “the appointment,” “the bill,” or “what I heard from my sister.” Then tell yourself, in plain language, that you will return to it at the time you picked. You are not deciding that it is silly, and you are not required to push it out of your mind. If it returns, you can make the same brief note again—or simply remind yourself of the appointment. Some worries are tied to real responsibilities, and postponing a longer look does not remove the responsibility. It makes room to choose a more deliberate moment for it. If the matter is urgent or time-sensitive, deal with it rather than waiting for the window.

A 2023 meta-analysis brought together seven randomized trials involving 999 participants. It found small effects of worry postponement on how long and how often people worried, while noting that long-term follow-up studies were lacking [1]. That is evidence for a modest possibility, not proof that the practice works for everyone or lasts indefinitely. In a 2025 randomized trial, 186 adults used an intervention over 14 days. The version that paired postponement with planning was associated with about 15 fewer reported minutes of worry than postponement alone; neither intervention significantly improved the measured sleep outcomes [2]. Those findings do not make a 10- or 15-minute window a clinically established dose. They do suggest why it may be useful to pair a later look with a concrete next step, while keeping expectations appropriately limited.
Set an appointment you can keep

Choose a time when you are usually able to pause, and begin with 10 to 15 minutes. That is a practical starting point, not a proven prescription. Pick a place where you can sit or stand comfortably, and use paper or a notes app—whatever is easy to find again. When a concern arises earlier in the day, capture only enough detail to remember it and name the time you will revisit it. At the appointment, review the list and choose one concern to examine. If nothing comes to mind, you do not have to invent a worry to fill the minutes. If the window feels too long, shorten it; if it consistently conflicts with real responsibilities, move it. The point is to make a small, repeatable container, not add another demanding task to the day.
Sort the worry into three parts

For the concern you choose, make three brief notes: what you know, what you are predicting, and what is within your influence. Suppose a friend has not replied. What you know might be only that there has been no reply yet. “They are angry with me” is a possible explanation, not a confirmed fact. Within your influence might be sending one clear follow-up, or deciding when you will check your phone again. This sorting is not a courtroom exercise: predictions are not foolish simply because they are uncertain, and the known facts may be incomplete. The purpose is to see which part of the concern is information, which part is an imagined outcome, and whether there is an action available now. Research on decentering—observing thoughts and emotions rather than treating them as the whole story—offers relevant context, but does not test this exact worry-window exercise [3].
Make one plan, or choose when to check

If there is a useful action, make it small and specific. An “if–then” plan connects a recognizable situation to a response: if the landlord has not confirmed the repair by Thursday afternoon, then I will send a concise follow-up. This does not guarantee the outcome; it gives your own next move a place on the page. If there is nothing useful to do yet, write when you will next check the situation, such as after a scheduled appointment or once a promised update is due. Then close the note. A plan can be as modest as gathering one document or asking one question. Avoid making the exercise a search for every possible risk or a demand that you reach certainty. Some problems do not have a complete answer today. A reasonable next step—or a defined time to reconsider—can be enough for this appointment.

A worry window is optional. If noting a concern makes it more vivid, if you find yourself extending the exercise into a long review, or if the practice leaves you feeling worse, stop or change course. You do not need to control your breathing, sit in a particular way or produce a neat conclusion. Nor should urgent safety concerns or decisions with real deadlines be deferred to preserve the exercise. The research base is limited: the meta-analysis found small effects and lacked long-term follow-up, and the newer trial did not find a sleep benefit [1][2]. This is a reflective tool, not a diagnosis or treatment. If worry is persistent, difficult to manage or interfering with daily life, consider speaking with a qualified health professional. Asking for support is not a failure of the practice; it is a different and often more appropriate next step.
Close the note beside the thing you were doing

Try the appointment once on a day when you have a little breathing room—not during a crisis, and not as a demand to fix everything on the page. Set a modest time, write down one recurring concern, and separate what is known from what is forecast. Choose one action or a specific time to check again, then close the notebook. Return to the ordinary scene that was already there: the dishes beside the sink, a book left open, someone waiting to finish a conversation. You might notice whether the worry has changed, or whether it is still present; neither result is a grade. The useful question is simply whether giving it a defined place made the rest of the moment easier to inhabit. Keep the experiment only if it serves you.
